newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: INTERVIEW-Malaysian city railway seeks riders.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Malaysian city railway seeks riders.

text.p: Motorists sitting in the evening gridlock in central Kuala Lumpur look up at the elevated blue and yellow box cars of Malaysia's first rapid rail transit system speeding by, and wish they were there.
And so does Zainal Abdul Ghani, chief executive officer of Sistem Transit Aliran Ringan Sdn Bhd (STAR), constructor and operator of the Light Rail Transit (LRT) system.
"Our ridership is less than forecasted, and so our break-even point is being pushed further back," Zainal told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday.

Forecasts in 1991 expected the average daily number of riders to be around 200,000. After seven months of operations, that figure stands at around 53,000 during weekdays and under 25,000 on weekends and public holidays.
Along with the new Kuala Lumpur International Airport, a new federal capital and a host of other undertakings, the LRT is one of the country's largest infrastructure development projects.

The sleek overhead railway is part of the futuristic look that Kuala Lumpur -- home to the world's tallest buildings, the 452 metre (1,482 feet) Petronas Twin Towers -- is unveiling when it hosts next year's Commonwealth Games, the most prestigious event held in Malaysia.
But the LRT has had its share of woes, including construction that has aggravated Kuala Lumpur's near gridlocked streets, work accidents and a sceptical public.
Members of parliament have complained that STAR's fares are too high.
A typical five-km (3.1 mile) trip costs 2.50 ringgit (95 cents). That's cheaper than a comparable four-ringgit taxi cab fare, but more expensive than taking a city bus.
Zainal says the relatively high fares are necessary to maintain standards.
"Those who can afford it get disillusioned by the unpredictability of existing public transport. It has to be reliable and safe. We have to ensure that it works."

Another reason STAR could not easily lower its fares is the huge cost of the project. The two phases are expected to cost a total of 3.5 billion ringgit, much of it from bank borrowings that have to be serviced monthly.
It is the world's first completely privatised urban rapid rail transit system, Zainal said, adding that he was taking a fresh look at STAR's financing.

A stock exchange listing would be a possibility under the government's special listing requirements for infrastructure companies. But Zainal says the public perception of STAR is not positive enough yet for a successful flotation.
Many viewed the LRT as Malaysia's shining hope for combating rising traffic congestion. Zainal said those expectations were too high.
"The LRT is one of the means to reduce traffic congestion, not the only one. You can't reduce congestion by the LRT alone," he said.
Lack of adequate feeder bus and taxi services to the LRT stations has also discouraged potential riders, Zainal said.
Kuala Lumpur's frequently uneven, or non-existent, footpaths are probably another reason why commuters prefer the drudgery of sitting behind their own steering wheels for hours a day.
STAR is the operator of one of five lines constituting an integrated urban transportation system for Kuala Lumpur that is expected to be completed by 2000.
More pressing, however, is the need to complete the second phase of STAR's own line in time for next September's Commonwealth Games.
"Ours is the only LRT going to the games village. We will have to be ready by the middle of next year, or you won't be seeing me in this seat at that time," said Zainal.
The second phase is progressing on time, he said.
($1 = 2.63 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-206 2323)
